summary: Lists mobility-related criteria to be considered when designing and choosing the Next Generation of IP, so that devices which move between networks could be supported. It was a contribution to the IPng selection process and is informational only.

plainLanguage.summary: If your laptop moves from place to place, the internet should still find it. This note lists what the new design should do for moving gadgets.

questions: criteria for choosing next generation ip
how do mobile devices keep their ip address while moving
what are bandwidth requirements for mobile ip
how should ipng support mobile hosts
subtitle: Design criteria for mobile hosts in the next-generation internet protocol

tldr.problem: Current internet protocols assume devices stay in one location, making it difficult for mobile hosts to maintain communications while moving between networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC establishes criteria for IPng designers in six categories: addressing (unique home addresses), communication (maintaining connections while moving), security (authentication and privacy), bandwidth (minimizing overhead on low-speed links), processing (supporting low-power processors), and message efficiency.
tldr.outcome: These criteria guided the design of Mobile IPv6, allowing mobile devices to keep their address while moving and maintain connectivity without loss of transport connections.

today: RFC 1688 is Informational and contributed to the Mobile IPv6 specification. Mobile IPv6 has been standardized but deployment remains limited due to challenges in implementation, carrier support, and the prevalence of workarounds like cellular carrier NAT.

sections.title: The Mobility Problem
sections.content:
Current internet protocols assume that a device's point of attachment to the network remains fixed. The IP address contains location information—its network number tells routers where to find the device. When a mobile node moves to a different network while keeping its IP address, the routing protocols cannot find it, and datagrams get lost.

This RFC specifies criteria that the next-generation IP protocol (IPng) should meet to support mobile hosts. The goal is to allow devices to move freely while maintaining communication, without requiring the device to change its IP address or lose existing transport connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet addresses contain location information, like street addresses. If you keep the same address but move to a different location, mail gets lost. The new internet needs to let devices move without losing their address or their connections.

sections.title: Addressing Requirements for Mobile Hosts
sections.content:
Mobile nodes must have a globally unique Home Address that identifies them to other nodes, regardless of where they currently attach to the network. The RFC specifies that ownership information in the address would be beneficial, allowing other nodes to determine the mobile node's topological location and supporting accounting records.

However, the Home Address must not contain topological information or manufacturer information that would hinder mobility. The addressing scheme must support automatic configuration since users cannot be expected to manually manage potentially thousands of mobile nodes. The RFC estimates that only 46 bits will be needed to densely number all mobile and home nodes worldwide, making efficient use of address space critical for bandwidth and processing efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: Every mobile device needs a permanent address that stays the same no matter where it is. The address should not include location details, and it must set itself up automatically without the user typing in numbers.

sections.title: Maintaining Connections While Mobile
sections.content:
A mobile node must continue communicating with other nodes even after moving to a different network. Mobile nodes using their Home Address must be able to resume communication after disconnection and reconnection at a different point of attachment, without loss of existing transport connections like TCP sessions.

When a mobile node moves, topological changes must not affect transport connections. For nodes that do not implement mobility functions, the changes should not be visible to them. For nodes that do implement mobility functions, they should be able to detect topological changes. The RFC specifies that mobile nodes are expected to change their point of attachment no more frequently than once per second, and changes occurring more frequently should be handled transparently at the link layer.
sections.plainLanguage: When you move your laptop to a different network, your email connection should keep working without interruption. The device should send out updates about where it is so people can still reach it.

sections.title: Security Requirements for Mobile Hosts
sections.content:
Mobility registration messages must be authenticated between the home topological repository and the mobile node. When correspondent nodes implement mobility functions and use redirection or path optimization, these must also be authenticated. The RFC addresses location privacy: while foreign administrations need not be aware of a mobile node's attachment, the home administration must be able to trace the current path to the mobile node's point of attachment.

Content privacy mechanisms must not be obscured by or depend on the topological location of mobile nodes. The RFC emphasizes that mobility must not create a less secure environment than the current Internet, and changes in topology must not affect inter-node security mechanisms. Anonymity is permitted but not required; mobility mechanisms must provide the ability to prevent anonymous attachment when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile devices need special codes to prove who they are when they register their new location. The home office should be able to find them, but foreign networks do not need to know where they are. Security should not get worse just because devices move.

sections.title: Bandwidth Efficiency for Low-Speed Links
sections.content:
Mobile nodes often operate on low-bandwidth links—HF radio limited by treaty to 1200 or 2400 bits per second, cellular radio at 2400 bps, and early digital cellular at 19,200 bps shared among many users. The RFC recognizes that bandwidth improvements cannot be assumed, so mobility mechanisms must work efficiently on current link technologies.

Administrative mobility messages must be kept as short as possible. Registration must not require more than a single request and reply, and the total registration message size must not exceed 120 bytes including link and internet headers. The RFC also notes that IPv4 datagram overhead of 40 bytes is already too large for acceptable response times on slow links. Therefore, IPng must add no more than 6 bytes of additional overhead per datagram. Van Jacobson header prediction, which compresses repetitive header fields, is essential for making low-speed links viable.
sections.plainLanguage: Slow radio connections need messages to be small and quick. The new internet should not add much extra data to each message, so typing responses stay fast enough to be usable.

sections.title: Processing Efficiency for Low-Power Devices
sections.content:
Mobile hosts often use low-speed processors—such as i86, i286, or i386 processors—and highly integrated components that cannot be readily upgraded. Datagram header fields that mobile nodes frequently examine must be in fixed locations with fixed sizes. Variable-length fields and fields that require complex shifts or prefix matches were explicitly rejected in the design of mobility headers.

The RFC specifies that field processing should primarily use simple equality tests rather than variable shifts and prefix matches, because the most prevalent mobile platforms use little-endian processors while network protocols use big-endian byte ordering. Fields that are not frequently examined, and whose content is not relevant in every message, should use Type-Length-Value format for flexibility without processing burden.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile devices often have older, slower processors. Headers must be simple and use fixed-size fields so low-power devices can process them quickly without getting hot or draining batteries.

references.text: Bradner, S., Ed., "IP: Next Generation (IPng) White Paper Solicitation", RFC 1550, December 1993.
